# Instructor guide · Topic 21: Bit Manipulation

<!-- generated by tools/export-docs.mjs from topics/ and questions/: do not edit by hand -->

## Learning objectives

Read and write numbers in binary, use &, |, ^, ~, > confidently, apply classic tricks (n & (n − 1), x & −x, XOR cancelling), and enumerate subsets with bitmasks.

By the end of the topic, students can:

- **Numbers in binary:** Computers store integers as bits.
- **The bitwise operators:** &, | and ^ combine two numbers column by column.
- **Masks: get, set, clear, toggle:** A mask is a number with 1s exactly where you want to act.
- **Classic tricks:** A few identities show up again and again: n & (n − 1) removes the lowest 1 bit, x & −x keeps only it, and x ^ x = 0 makes pairs vanish.
- **Subsets as bitmasks:** With n items, the numbers 0 ..

## Duration and prerequisites

- Lessons: about **60 minutes** of guided material (5 lessons)
- Practice: 14 coding problems and 23 quick questions in the bank; plan at least as much practice time as lesson time
- Suggested format: one 90-minute session
- Prerequisites: Topic 1 (Python for DSA), Topic 3 (Algorithmic Thinking)

## Live coding demonstrations

- Binary in Python (lesson “Numbers in binary”)
- The four operations (lesson “Masks: get, set, clear, toggle”)
- Brute force → optimal walkthrough: **Single number: counting → XOR** (Challenge tab). Code the brute force, ask students to find the repeated work, then refactor.
- Visualizers to drive while students predict the next step: Bitwise operators, bit by bit

## Questions to ask the class

Ask, wait for several answers, then reveal (the answers are on the topic's Review flashcards).

- 13 in binary?
- Get bit i?
- Set / clear / toggle bit i?
- n & (n − 1)?
- x & −x?
- x ^ x? x ^ 0?
- ~x in Python?
- All subsets of n items?

### Teaching notes

- Have students verify each trick on paper with 4-bit numbers before coding. Ask: why is x & −x the lowest set bit? (Two’s complement: −x = ~x + 1.)

## Classroom exercises (individual, 10–15 minutes each)

- Number of 1 Bits (`bit-count-ones`)
- Power of Two (`bit-power-two`)
- Single Number (`bit-single`)

Code tracing on the board: bin() and int(…, 2) (`bit-p1`), AND, OR, XOR (`bit-p2`), Shifts (`bit-p3`), Bitwise NOT in Python (`bit-p4`)

Find-the-bug warm-ups: Zero is not a power of two (`bit-d1`), Testing the wrong bit (`bit-d2`)

## Pair programming (25–30 minutes)

One driver types, one navigator thinks ahead and checks edge cases; swap every 10 minutes.

- Counting Bits 0..n (`bit-counting-bits`)
- Reverse 32 Bits (`bit-reverse`)

## Homework

- Gray Code (`bit-gray`)
- Add Without + (`bit-add`)
- Single Number II (`bit-single-ii`)
- Write is_power_of_four(n) with one mask.
- Enumerate all subsets of [1..10] with sum 15 using bitmasks, and compare with a backtracking version from topic 10.
- Finish the topic's Review quiz in the browser and clear the revision queue.

## Solutions and grading

- Reference solutions: `solutions/21_bits/` (also behind “Show solution” in the browser).
- Students check their own work with `python dsa.py test <id>`; collect `pytest tests/test_my_solutions.py -k bits` output as evidence.
- Grade with the coding rubric in [README.md](README.md#grading-rubrics).
